points.title: Who the early voters are
points.caption: lean of early voters by primary history, a proxy for party, through Fri 23 Oct: effectively even, a description of who voted, not how; 29.3% have no primary on record

fig.source: theoelections early vote by primary history (SOS rosters matched to SOS primary rosters)
fig.note: Basis A: any of the four primaries 2020-2026, the same set for every year. Cumulative early vote including mail. 2026 re-read 25 Oct: theoelections data file of 05:15 UTC; day 5 (Fri 23 Oct) complete in 249 of 254 counties.

points.sentence: By primary history (which party's primaries a voter has taken part in, a proxy for party and not a vote), early voters with a Republican primary history now match those with a Democratic one, a lean of 0.2 points Republican (11.7 points Republican at this point in 2024); the first days leaned Democratic, which is consistent with regular primary voters voting first, the usual shape of early voting, and Friday's new voters leaned 3.0 points Republican, against 5.5 points Democratic on Monday.

points.title: Why "Democrats are surging" headlines can mislead
points.caption: change since the 2022 midterm in the gap between registered Democrats' and Republicans' shares of early ballots, same point, in the 22 states that report early ballots by party (the 2022 ElectProject set, its 30 Oct 2022 capture)

fig.source: UF Election Lab: 2026 early vote, the 22 states that report by party (state files summed)
fig.note: The same 22 states, each from its own 2026 file, on the same day as the 2022 figure (rebuilt by the national early-vote slice; re-checked by the verifier).

points.sentence: The 2024 early vote was the most Republican of any year shown, so against 2024 every state in our party-reporting table looks far more Democratic; measured against the 2022 midterm instead, those 22 states moved 2.5 points combined (D+12.2 then, D+14.7 now; 1.0 to 2.7 allowing one day of misalignment), and with Texas mail ballots down 24.8% from 2024, in-person "records" overstate the total. Neither year is a clean baseline (Republicans are being urged to vote early this year, and some states have changed their early-vote rules), and ballots by party say who voted, not how.

points.title: What the polls missed before
points.caption: how far 2024 Senate polls in Texas leaned too Democratic

fig.source: Wikipedia, 2024 Texas Senate election (poll table and result)
fig.note: Mean of (actual R margin minus poll R margin), polls in the final 31 days, one row per poll. Positive = polls too Democratic.

points.sentence: Texas polls ran too Democratic in 2020 and 2024 (4.9 points in the 2024 Senate race); in 2022 the governor average was close (RealClearPolitics had Abbott up 10.4, he won by 10.9), though a simple mean of the listed polls ran 3.1 points too Democratic; in 2018 they ran too Republican by 3.4 points, so a miss can run either way.

points.title: What the fake-poll story is, and is not
points.caption: the most that removing the two exposed firms that polled Texas moves any Texas poll average

fig.source: Wikipedia, 2026 United States Senate election in Texas (poll table)
fig.note: Texas averages (R minus D), one row per poll, with and without the SoCal and Wedgewood polls. Same computation as the poll table in section 6.

points.sentence: Four polling firms were exposed this year (two admitted inventing polls, one admitted moving respondents toward a candidate whose campaign, records show, had paid it, one went dark without admitting anything), but taking out the two that polled Texas moves no Texas average by more than 0.28 points.

figs.source: Wikipedia, 2026 United States Senate election in Texas (poll table)
figs.note: Texas averages (R minus D), one row per poll, with and without the SoCal and Wedgewood polls. Same computation as the poll table in section 6.

figs.value: Admitted fabricating nearly all of its surveys after FiftyPlusOne confronted it; said one crowdfunded Nebraska poll was real and called itself an "experimental project".
figs.source: FiftyPlusOne, 2026-10-20: "FiftyPlusOne just caught a pollster faking data"

figs.value: Admitted to the Los Angeles Times that its published results were fake; its website called the polls a "short-term social experiment". Withdrew its LA mayor, Wisconsin and Nevada releases.
figs.source: AP via PBS NewsHour, 2026-08-19: what to know about the fake election poll numbers

figs.value: Admitted reassigning some respondents who picked Jay Collins to James Fishback, the Florida Republican primary candidate whose campaign had paid it $1,575. FiftyPlusOne banned it permanently.
figs.source: FiftyPlusOne, 2026-08-20: suspending two pollsters for ethics violations

figs.value: Took down its website, Substack and X account by the morning of 22 October, two days after FiftyPlusOne interviewed a SoCal-affiliated person and a few days after it asked to verify SoCal's data. It has not admitted anything.
figs.source: FiftyPlusOne, 2026-10-22: "More pollster funny business uncovered"

points.title: Who is still left to vote
points.caption: reliable Republican and Democratic primary voters (3 or 4 of the four 2018 to 2024 primaries) who have not voted yet; the tracker covers 243 of 254 counties

fig.source: Transparency USA / JPM Strategies Texas turnout tracker (primary-history pools)
fig.note: Voters with 3 or 4 of the four 2018 to 2024 primaries on record who have not yet voted. TUSA update of 24 Oct 4:46 PM CT, 243 of 254 counties.

points.sentence: Of the 2.24 million Republican and 1.91 million Democratic primary voters who have not voted, the most reliable split 688K to 351K, a reservoir that can show up rather than votes in hand (a primary vote is not a November vote): the Republican count includes March primary voters who backed Cornyn against Paxton, both parties' March early voters have turned out at about the same rate (56.6% and 57.3%), and voters with no primary history are about half of the votes still to come (49% in the public model's middle case).

points.title: What past elections say about the polls and the early vote
points.caption: how far toward Democrats the final polls missed, on average, in 26 past state races

fig.source: Federal Election Commission: certified results (Federal Elections 2012 to 2022, 2024 presidential results), the results the backtest scores against
fig.note: Computed by Intellz (backtest of 25 Oct): each read uses only the early vote that existed at the same point before past elections and is scored against the certified result (FEC, state canvasses); the polls are 538's final averages or the mean of the final 21 days of polls. The cases cluster in a few states (Maine and North Carolina supply many), so these are descriptions of past cases and no interval is claimed.

points.sentence: Tested on past state races with only the early vote known 10 to 13 days out: the final polls missed toward Democrats by 2.0 points on average over 26 races. A turnout read built from early ballots beat the polls when each midterm was compared with the last midterm (3.7 points off against 4.0, 8 races), and in Texas the primary-history read missed by 1.95 over 4 cycles. The stat the media leans on most, the party-registration lead in the early vote, missed the result by 16.0 points on average over 18 races.

figs.source: Federal Election Commission: certified results (Federal Elections 2012 to 2022, 2024 presidential results), the results the backtest scores against
figs.note: Computed by Intellz (backtest of 25 Oct): each read uses only the early vote that existed at the same point before past elections and is scored against the certified result (FEC, state canvasses); the polls are 538's final averages or the mean of the final 21 days of polls. The cases cluster in a few states (Maine and North Carolina supply many), so these are descriptions of past cases and no interval is claimed.

figs.value: Texas 2024: certified Trump margin 13.68 points (FEC 2024 results); the turnout read 11 days out said 6.60, the final 538 average 7.63.
